utterances.text: It is one place, but Streliste -- by Streliste is the place where the garbage dump was, whereas this other place is a little bit far from Suhareka, 300, 400 metres far, before you go to the garbage place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. But both graves were located at one location; do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And how now, after all these years, what label or what place name would you give to these two graves? Because, as I said, throughout your testimony a couple of different words were used for that location. How do you wish to have this location be described today?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That place is in Lubishte, below the police checking point. Both villages have two different names. I cannot change them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell me which of the names I read to you are villages, first of all.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lubishte is one, Korishe is the another, whereas the garbage is near Shpinadjinadi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... asking for the garbage dump now. Following up on what you said, is it correct to say that the location of the graves is in between the place Lubishte -- the villages of Lubishte and the villages of Korishe?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: At the place which you encircled here on P277 and marked with a 1?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's approximately, because it's a map, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to move on to some questions of my learned friend relating to Pusto Selo. He had mentioned or put to you that tests had been performed in Pusto Selo on the bodies -- on the hands of the exhumed bodies. He had mentioned that the bodies were covered with sheets and blankets in Pusto Selo and that markings were put on the bodies once exhumed. He had also put to you that the exhumed bodies were put into body-bags. Do you remember having received these questions?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What I want to ask you now is if I put you now to the firing range and to the garbage dump, could you answer the following questions: That night when the bodies were exhumed at both places, were there any tests performed on the hands of these exhumed bodies?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Were there -- were the bodies, before they were loaded onto the truck by you, covered with any sheets or blankets?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were simply dressed in civilian clothes, the way they had -- happened to be dressed when they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So you did not put any blankets around them before you loaded them on the truck, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And did you or somebody else put any markings on these bodies before they were put on the refrigerator truck?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And did the bodies were put into body-bags at the firing range or at the garbage dump --

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before you loaded them onto the refrigerator truck?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to finally address one small issue relating to the photo parade touched upon by my learned colleague. Page 18, lines 18 to 22 of today's transcript, you were asked about the proofing we too had a couple of days ago and about the camouflage photo-board. Could I ask you, did I show you a black-and-white photo-board or a coloured photo-board on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a coloured photo-board.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I could have the 65 ter number 2375 being shown, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to respond promptly. This exhibit has been replaced. We received 2375 -- did I hear that correctly? It was submitted to us as a replacement on the 3rd of February, 2007, at 1700 hours, and I already said that in the additional statement it was indicated that the witness was shown Prosecution Exhibit 5162, and that is not the pre-trial number. It was given after the pre-trial brief was submitted. It's an exhibit that I believe is a depiction of uniforms that an investigator of the Tribunal or, rather, of the OTP showed the witness - I may be mistaken now, it may have been either in February or in June 2000 - where it was already stated what uniforms are depicted. My learned friend the Prosecutor is right, this exhibit is in colour, the previous one was black and white, but the previous exhibit contained marks, markings by the witness who recognised the uniforms. But the uniforms were in the same order, they were depicted in the same order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want to add something to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Very briefly. The only point I think is made already, that no black-and-white picture or photo-board was ever shown to this witness - my learned colleague also understood that - but only a colour photo-board. That's the only short statement I would have at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will take into account what my learned friend has just told us, but then I don't understand why the Exhibit 5162 was replaced and was now assigned this number, the number that was provided by my colleague now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I can give you an explanation for that, and I could even walk the witness through that. The previous 65 ter number 5162 was shown to the witness. It is a colour photograph. However -- and that's also how we informed my learned colleague two days ago, why I e-mailed. The technical quality of that photos were of a very low value. In other words, the camouflage colours, as they are depicted on this exhibit right now in front of Your Honours, is of a higher quality so that one can distinguish the camouflage pattern on it. On this previous exhibit, 65 ter number 5162, when we made a colour print-out and tried to use it with the witness, we basically saw on the print-out itself it did not have any camouflage patterns any longer because of the poor quality of the exhibit as such. Once we had found that out by showing it for the first time to the witness, we showed him a proper quality image, which is now in front of Your Honours, and asked then the question to the witness. And having just undergone that exercise a few days ago, we immediately endeavoured to inform the Defence, as we did, about that fact, that we are seeking to replace the colour photo-board which is of a poor quality with a high-quality picture depicting exactly the same uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I've just one last question, Witness, to you. At the time when we showed you the colour photocopy, were there any markings next to one of these camouflage patterns, when it was shown to you?

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So, in fact, after you told us that this is the uniform of Jova and this is the uniform pattern of Budimir Spasic, you were given an opportunity to mark where you believed that the camouflage pattern of the uniform of both men was.

utterances.speaker: ALI GJOGAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Neuner. You will be pleased to know that that completes the questions for you. The Chamber is thankful that you've come to The Hague and thankful for the assistance that you've been able to give us. You may now leave, and the court officer will give you directions where to go. Thank you, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next Prosecution witness is Mr. Mustafa Dragaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This witness will be testifying about the allegations in paragraph 72(C), 75(F), Schedule F, and paragraph 77 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you solemnly declare that the evidence you will give to this Tribunal will be the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz will now ask some questions of you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Mustafa Dragaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you're a Kosovo Albanian from the village of Lecina in Srbica or Skenderaj municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In March 1999, sir, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: In March 1999 I lived in Leqina, until war started.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were most people in the village of Lecina Kosovo Albanians like yourself, or was this a mixed village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Most of us were Albanians. There were a few Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How big was the village of Lecina at the time? Approximately how many houses did it have?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: About 100 houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I want to start by asking you some questions about events that took place in Lecina on 25th March, 1999. Do you recall what, if anything, extraordinary --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I remember. I remember they started to set fire to Leqina on the 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who started to -- I was starting to ask you about events that took place in Lecina on the 25th of March, 1999. Do you recall what, if anything extraordinary, happened during that time? And, sir, I would ask you to wait until I finish asking my question before you start answering, just so the interpreters can interpret your questions back into English -- your answers back into English.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: On the 25th they shelled our village from Bellanica, Leqina. They shelled also -- my house on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "they shelled the village," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: The Serb police and army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say they shelled your village, is this something you were able to observe yourself from your house?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I didn't see it, but from my house you can see that it was in the direction of Bellanica because nobody could dare and go there and see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say that it was in the direction of Belanica, are you referring to the direction from which the shells were coming?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. They came from Bellanica on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you recall for how long the village of Belanica was shelled on the 25th of March?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: It lasted for about two hours. I didn't have a watch.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I understand. At the time, where were you in the village when this shelling was going on?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: On the 25th I was in Leqina. On the 26th I left Leqina at about 5.00 in the afternoon. The others left in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Why did you decide to leave Lecina on the 26th of March?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Because they were burning our houses and shelling it, and all went to Izbica and gathered there because we thought we would feel safer there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Again, when you say they were burning your houses, who are you referring to by "they"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Whoever, other than the Serbian police and army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Why did you decide to go to Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Because we felt safer, because in Izbica at that time there were no Serbs, and it was a village inhabited by Albanians. The mountain was close by.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you decided to leave on the 26th, was it just you and your family who left, or did other people in your village also leave Lecina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I was with my family, but my sons and their wives left earlier. Myself and my wife left in the afternoon, at 5.00, but the neighbours also left. The entire village left.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And did the entire village head in the same direction as you and your wife, that is, to Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, they went to Izbica, all of them. Most had left earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you tell us that you went to Izbica on the 26th. When you got there, where were you housed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: On a meadow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was there anyone else on that meadow with you, other than you and your family?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, they were people from Leqina, Klina e Begut, Blazin, Kernica. I don't know how many people were there from how many villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how big was this meadow where you were staying? Just roughly.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: It was quite big.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know roughly how big it was?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: About 2 hectares, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you said there were people from other villages there. Were they all staying in this same 2 hectares, this meadow, with you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. All of us stayed there, but the people who had their houses there stayed in their own homes. The 28th, they also came to the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who also came to the meadow on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: The Serb police and army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And between the 26th and the 28th of March, did you remain on the -- in this meadow?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: On the 26th in the evening, I went there. On the 27th we remained there all day. On the 28th the Serb police and army came, on the 28th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what were the conditions like on this meadow during the two days that you remained there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: On the 27th during the day, it was good, but in the evening it started to rain. It rained all night.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And were you just outdoors or were you under some sort of shelter or protection on the meadow?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: We were outdoors. We stayed in the rain. There was no where I could go to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you say that on the 28th of March the Serb police and army came. Do you recall from which direction they came?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: They came from Leqina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And approximately how many Serb police and army were in this group that came from Lecina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I don't know. There were many, but I cannot give you an accurate number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was it more than ten, less than ten? Was it a large group, a small group?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: 2, 300 maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did this group of Serb police and army approach the group where you were in the meadow?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. They came to where we were sitting, males, females, children. And they started to separate the males from the others, those, the young ones; and the others, they asked us to form a line on the meadow. And then they asked us to give them money. They cursed us and they threw down our caps. And then they asked us, You can get back your caps. Whoever had money on him or on her gave them money. I didn't have any on me, so I didn't give them any. They struck me on my left eye. Then they started to -- today it's Bajram day, and according to custom you had to slaughter a sheep. And then they said, We will slaughter you today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: May I stop you there, sir. You said that you were sitting, males, females, and children. Were there any men of military age among the villagers that were in the meadow with you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Not of military age. I would say maybe two or three. Hajriz Draga was about 40. One from Kline e Ulet was also of about the same age. I don't know the exact age. But the others were all younger, about 12 or 13 years and less.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where were the younger men, the men of military age? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: The young men were in the woods, on the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Why were they in the woods?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Not to be killed by the Serbian police and army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And why did you decide to remain in the meadow and not go to the woods with the younger men?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Because I thought they would not kill us. Had I known that this was their intention, I would have joined them in the woods, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that they approached you, and they asked you to give them money. Did any other persons -- because you said --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said you didn't have any money yourself, but did any other persons in your group hand over money to the Serb police and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, there were. They were a little bit further from me. Some who gave money were killed. Sadik Hoti, who gave 500 DM, was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you said that they cursed you and threw down your caps. What exactly did they say to you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: They were swearing at us. They were cursing Rugova, Thaci. I couldn't understand very well because they were cursing in Serbian. And in the end they started to count the group from the right-hand side, and they directed one part of the group to the west and the other to the east. So the group that was directed to the west started to go upwards, and we who were in the group directed to the east were directed towards some woods. And then they said to us, Turn in this direction, and as soon as they turned, they opened gun-fire. Hajriz Draga was immediately caught by a bullet. He fell over me. I remained there for some 20 or 30 minutes. And Hajzer had reached the woods, and I crawled, too, towards the woods. And once in the woods I turned my head back and saw everybody lying down on the fields. Sadik Tahiri, who was alive after the shooting but who died later after two hours, told me that he gave them 500 Deutschemarks for his life, but they killed him anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to stop you there, if we can go back briefly. You said they separated the men from the women and children. What happened to the women and children? Where were they sent?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: The women were directed towards Vojnika and Turicevce. They were separated from us. After the women left, they executed us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you said that the men were divided into two groups. One was sent east, and the other one was sent to the west. How many men --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How many men were in your group?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I didn't count them, but there were quite many. As I said, nobody dared to look back or look on the sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "quite many," does this mean more than ten, less than ten, 15? About how many were in your group?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: No, no, not less than 60 or 70. More, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us that your group was directed to the east, towards some woods. Who directed you to go to the east, towards the woods?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: The person who divided the group, the larger group, into two groups, he told the others to take one group to this direction and the other to the other direction. So these persons, after they carried out the execution, they went back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can you describe this person who instructed others to divide the group? What did he look like, this person, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Ten years have passed. I'm old so my memory doesn't serve me right. But he was kind of a chubby person, dark, of average build.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was he wearing any kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. They were all wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall the colour of the uniform he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I've forgotten the colours. Both police and military colours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well. Now, when you were taken towards the woods, was anyone escorting your group?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: They escorted us. Nobody else. That was exactly why they were taking us into that direction, to execute us, not for fun.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dragaj, when you say they escorted you, who are you referring to by "they"?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: The police, the army. The Serbian police and army. Nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived to the woods where you were being escorted?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: The execution happened before we reached the woods. When we were next to the woods, they started to execute us. Those who were in the back, in the rear part, they were already executed while in the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Other than yourself, did anyone else survive this execution?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Hajriz Draga, Sheremet Krasniqi, and Rrustem Hoti.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Is this person Hajriz Draga different from the person who you told us earlier who fell on top of you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Hajriz is the person who fell on my body, while this is Hajriz, another person, Hajzer, correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what happened to this person who fell on your body, Hajriz? Did he survive as well?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: For awhile. He died later because nobody could give him any help. He asked me for some water, but there was no where I could get water. I wasn't in good condition myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were you injured in the shooting?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did you know any of the persons who were killed in this execution?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Most of them I did. There were also people whom I didn't know. There were people from Puzine, Kline e Ulet, from Gllareva, from everywhere, and from some villages that I have never even heard of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Of those whom you did know, where were they from?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: From Leqina, some from Puzine, some from Kline, some from Gllareva, some from Kernica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of those persons who were killed in your group? Only those you recall I'm asking about.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I remember some of them. Some I've forgotten. Less than the half I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us the names of those that you still remember?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Those that I have not forgotten, I can. Halim Shala, Ren Shala, Idriz Shala, Sali Shala, Kujtim Shala, Rexh Qelaj, Metush Qelaj, Smajl Qelaj, Murat Draga, Ali Draga, Ismet Draga, Hajriz Draga, Rrustem Draga, Cen Draga, Iljaz Dervisi, Sali Dervisi, Iljaz Bajra, Bajram Bajra, Kajtaz Islami, and others that I've forgotten. There were also women killed, but they were killed on route, not at the site of the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this is a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very good. We'll adjourn now and resume again at 1.00. We'll have a break now for half an hour to enable you to have a rest, and we'll continue at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you say, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Mr. Dragaj, before the break you gave us the list of names of the persons you remembered were killed in that incident that you've been describing. Were any of the persons who were killed in your group dressed in any kind of military attire or uniform?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: No. Civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: At the time when this massacre occurred you were approximately 60 years old; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Around 60 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there any other men in your group of your same age?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, there were, and there were also older than me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, you told us that another one of the men in your group fell on top of you and that's how you survived. What did you do after the shooting stopped?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I remained there for some 20 minutes, lying on the ground. Hajriz was on top of me. After some 20 minutes I looked up. Musli Hajra was in the woods. He was alive. He called me, he said, Come to the woods because they are burning houses and everything they find down there. So I crawled to the woods, and when I looked back in the direction of the meadow, I saw those who had been killed lying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: For how long did you remain in the woods?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: On the 28th of March, that's the date of the execution, and we remained in the mountains, in the woods, till 31st of March, when these people who had been killed were buried.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You had told us that the group that had arrived in Izbica was approximately of 200, 300 policemen and soldiers. For how long did they remain in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: They remained there from 28th till the 30th. They left on the 30th, in the evening and went to Vojnika, Broja. That's where they had their place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you just told us that you returned on the 31st of March, and that's to Izbica, and that's when the people who were killed were buried. Did you participate in the burial of those who were killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. Until the 31st of March I was there in the woods around Izbica the whole time. And on the 31st of March, whoever could take part in the burial, took part; myself, my sons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, you told us earlier that the group of men had been split into two groups, and you have already explained what happened to your group. Do you know what happened to the other group that was taken towards the west of the village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: All from the other group were killed. Two or three, I think, only survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how do you know that those persons in the other group were killed?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: When we carried the bodies we found them all killed on the ground on the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And was there anything particular that you remember about the bodies that you found of that group that was taken to the west of the village? Was there anything that struck your mind about this -- the men that you found that had been killed there in the west of the village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: They were killed, all of them. It was difficult even to carry these bodies because of the state they were in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And what state was that, that these bodies were in?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Some could not recognise their own family members, their fathers or sons. It was only through their clothes that we could identify them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Why couldn't they be recognised? What had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Most of them were shot in their heads. Secondly, they remained without being buried for a long time, and they were decomposed. That's why it was difficult for people to recognise their own family members.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were any of the men in that second group dressed in any sort of military attire or uniform?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: There were no soldiers or people dressed in uniforms on that day or the previous days. These were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You had told us that in your group there were other men of your age and even older than you. Was that also the case of the men who were taken in the other direction, those who were taken west and killed there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. There were people of my age and older than me, too. There was a disabled person in the second group called Hetem. He didn't have one of his legs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you know the full name of this disabled person who was in the second group? Do you know the last name?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Hetem Osmanaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now you mentioned earlier that there had been also women killed. In which --

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: They were killed on route as they were travelling, not at the place where the men were killed. Zada Dragaj, who was 105 years old, was killed. Another woman who was 90 years old was killed. Also Zoje Osmana was burned. Shala Sali, Saban Musliu, they were all burned with their things in the tractors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And where were they burned? Was this also in the village or outside the village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: They were burned in their tractors on the meadow, not in their houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: In total, approximately how many people were killed that day, on 28th March, in Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Approximately, and from the number of bodies we buried, 147. We buried that day 147 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Where were these bodies buried?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: They were buried in Izbica. A man gave one of his meadows. They were not buried in the cemetery but in the meadow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When did this burial take place?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: On the 31st of March. It was a Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there any members of the KLA present during the burial of the victims of this massacre?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Two or three, I would say, because most of them had their fathers amongst people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And do you know how it is that members of the KLA came to take part in the burial of these victims?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: In my opinion they came here because they had to bury their own family members - father or uncle or brother. It was very dangerous to bury these victims. There was a lot of movement in Broja and Vojnika, and they were not buried properly as human beings are. They were buried like animals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Were there any markings made in the place where the victims were buried, any markings that allowed to identify who was buried there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: A piece of wood was placed on each and every victim -- location where the victim was buried and numbers were placed on this wood, 1, 2, 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did these pieces of wood also have the name of each one of the victims that was buried there?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, names were written.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how were the different victims identified? How did you know which name to put in each tomb for the victims?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: For example, this was done so that every person was identified. So every grave was given a name, a name of a person that was buried in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And who helped identify the victims?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Family members of those who had been killed took note of this; for example, this person is buried in grave number 1 and this, in grave number 2. And the same pattern was followed until all the bodies were buried.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was anyone in particular in charge of compiling the list of names of the victims of the massacre?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Sadik Xhemajli looked like the person in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who was this person, Sadik Xhemajli?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Sadik Xhemajli was from Izbica, and he was a KLA member. I think he has appeared before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, after the burial took place, what did you do? Did you remain at Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: After the burial and when the forces withdrew, the Serbian forces, I stayed in the mountains or woods of Izbica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Until the forces withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Just a clarification from your answer. For how long did you remain in the mountains or woods of Izbica after the burial took place?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I don't know the date when the forces withdrew, but as soon as they withdrew from Vojnika and Broja area, the following day I went to Leqina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: When you say "the forces withdrew," which forces are you referring to that withdrew from this area?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I refer to the Serbian forces, the Serbian police and army. There were no other forces there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've told us where the bodies of the victims were buried. Are those bodies still at this location in Izbica, in this field where they were buried?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: No. They were exhumed from the 28th of May and onwards. For four or five days they were being removed from the graves. They didn't leave a single body there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who exhumed the bodies of the victims from the grave?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: The Serbian police and army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How do you know that the bodies were exhumed? Was this something you observed yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: This I know because on the 31st of March I took part in the burial of these victims. On the 28th of May they began the removal of these bodies from the graves, and they didn't leave a single body there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I'll repeat my question: Was this something you observed yourself, these exhumations of the bodies of the victims?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I was in the woods of Izbica every day. During the day they would shell and then they would enter with their infantry into the villages. So the day when they removed the bodies, they started with the shelling. There was some hills there, and you could see it clearly from those hills that they were working on these graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Who did you see was working on these graves, from where you were located?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I could see that it was the Serbian police and army. Nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, do you know where these bodies were taken, the bodies of the victims that were exhumed from Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: No, I don't, but I know that some victims from the Izbica massacre were found in Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the two other locations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand your answer. Could you repeat the locations where the bodies of these victims were found?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: The bodies of those killed, I don't know where they were taken on that particular moment. But later on these bodies, some were found in Mitrovic, Suhadoll, somewhere near Vushtrri and at Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How do you know that these bodies were found at these locations? How did you obtain this information?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: The body of the brother of my daughter-in-law was found in Batajnica. He was buried in the fifth grave in Izbica. So every body that was found, later on people were told where it was found.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could you give us the name of the brother of your daughter-in-law that was found in Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Fatmir Osmani.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, sir, after the Serbian forces withdrew from Kosovo, did you return to your village of Lecina?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in what condition did you find your house in the village?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: It was leveled with the ground. It was burned and completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What about the other houses in the village? In what condition were they?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: The whole village was burnt and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic, do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Dragaj. My name is Veljko Djurdjic, and I'm on the Defence team of Vlastimir Djordjevic; together with me is Ms. Marie O'Leary. And I have some questions for you regarding your evidence today. Mr. Mustafa, could you please spell your name for us.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I think I can. M-u-s-t-a-f-a.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's your first name. And your last name, please.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: D-r-a-g-a-j.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So your last name is Dragaj, not Draga; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, with a "J" at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dragaj, do you remember that you gave a statement on the 11th and the 13th of November, 1999, to an investigator of the OTP, of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I have given statements, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the statement was read out to you in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. They read it to me in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you signed every page of the statement and the certification that is part of the statement on the 13th of November, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I remember I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 8th of March, 2002, you signed a declaration stating that the contents of your statement is true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge and belief, that this was the basis of your statement; and that an officer of the Registry of the International Tribunal certified that statement?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Do you remember that you were warned that false testimony might incur action against you, that there might be proceedings against you, and that then you signed the declaration?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dragaj, in the statement that I have in front of me - the date is the 13th of November, 1999 - it is stated that you served -- that you did your national service -- national service in the JNA in Karlovac, Modrica, and Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragaj, could you please tell me, if you recall, what year did you do your national service and what was the last town where you served?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. In 1958, February, I went to do the military service. In 1960, the 2nd of June, I finished it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what colour uniform you wore during your national service?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I don't remember that. It was like green, grass green, but many years have passed ever since so I have forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your recollection is excellent. Could you please tell us, the uniforms that you saw during the time that you told us about today, what colour were those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I have forgotten all the colours. I didn't even look at the colours. First, I was not interested; second, I was afraid. I didn't dare look up at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can I then conclude that you did not dare look at the forces that entered the village, as you've just told us, that you were much too afraid to do that?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: My village? I don't understand "your village." You mean my village or Izbica?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I meant Izbica.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: In Izbica I didn't dare to look at them, I told you, because when you see that people are shooting at you, want to execute you, I don't think anyone would dare look at the executors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it the case that you did not dare to look at them even before that because you were too afraid?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Since 1997 I didn't dare look at them. I did my best to avoid them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But could you please tell us why, from 1997, you didn't look at them? Did anything happen; and if yes, what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. They came in 1997 and took me from my yard to the police station, and they beat me up there. They asked me for weapons, but I didn't possess any weapons. When my household people didn't know that they took me away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. Did they take you away because you had the weapons or because you didn't have the weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: They took me to ask me for a weapon, thinking that I possessed a weapon. And they took me to the police station and beat me up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, did you have weapons, or did you not have weapons? Could you please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: If I had a weapon, I would have handed it over to them right away when they came to my yard. Why should I go to the police station with them?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true what it says here in your statement, that you had ten children; eight sons and two daughters?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is it true that four of your sons at the relevant time in 1999, in other words, from March until the Serb forces pulled out, as you told us, that four of your sons lived in Germany?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Since when have they been living in Germany?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: One went there when he was 15 years old or so -- 15 or so years ago. The others went before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that your sons Sheqir, Bedri, Fahria and Elmi remained with you?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: They lived for awhile, but Bedri and Elmi went to Montenegro; Sheqir and Fahria to Albania. The Serb forces came.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragaj, I was asking you about the time before the air-strikes began. Did they live together with you in the same household at that time, or did they have their own homes?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: They lived in the same household.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they married?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Bedri and Sheqir, yes. The other two married after the war, Elmi and Fahria.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether you lived in several houses or in a single house?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I lived in one house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And the sons who were married and the unmarried sons and the daughter?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, they all lived with me. The other daughter is in Germany for 12, 13 years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Could you tell me, that means that there existed only one house where all of you lived?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was one house, and still there is one house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether there was a wall around this house?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: Yes. There was a wall built with blocks of concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how high this wall was?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I didn't measure it, but the house is three storeys high.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: If somebody were to pass by your house, could they see what was happening in your house and in your yard because of the wall?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: But you can look at the yard because there are windows. Some windows -- some rooms have windows; some do not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragaj, I was asking you about people outside of the wall. Could they see what was happening in your house and in your yard from the outside, given that there was a wall?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: I don't understand what you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could somebody easily go over the wall and into your yard?

utterances.speaker: MUSTAFA DRAGAJ
utterances.text: There is no wall and no fence around my yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have five minutes left. I would like us to stop the cross-examination now because I have an important housekeeping matter to raise of great importance for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will then adjourn for the day. Mr. Dragaj, we've got to finish hearing evidence today at this point, and we continue again tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the morning. The court officer will show you out, and we look forward to hearing the rest of your evidence tomorrow morning, if you could come then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, as you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry I have to interrupt the witness before the end of our session today, but today at two minutes past 12.00, the Defence was notified about a change in the order of the witnesses to be called. And the change is of such a nature that the witness who was supposed to be examined today or tomorrow will now be called some other week, and the witness who was supposed to be heard in the week after the 9th of February is supposed to be called tomorrow. I have to give you an overview of the time-line of this problem. In accordance with the decision of the Trial Chamber, the Defence is to receive the witness list for any given week two weeks before they're to be called. We received a list on the 13th of January from the Prosecution. The first on the list is Veton Surroi, then K83, and then Mr. Gjogaj, followed by Mr. Dragaj. Then on the 19th of January we received the following list with Ms. Shyhrete Berisha, Nike Peraj, Loshi Liri, and Lizane, that's the last witness. On the 26th of January, we were told that in the week from the 9th of February, we will hear Avdyli Mehmet, Krasniqi Mehmet, Ramadani Lufti, and John Paul Sweeney. On the 2nd of February, we received notification that Avdyli Mehmet, Krasniqi, Ramadani Lufti, and Paul Sweeney will be heard in the week after the 16th of February. You know that the Defence has agreed to the change and agreed to hear Mrs. Berisha after Veton Surroi. It caused us great problems. Because of our manpower and organisational problems, we cannot deal with such reshuffling of witnesses. We cannot do our job in a way that will ensure an efficient trial and a proper defence for Mr. Djordjevic. So the witness who is notified for the week after the 16th, now all of a sudden is to be called tomorrow after witness Mustafa Dragaj. We are unable to deal with that, and I think, and I'm calling on the Chamber to reject this and to see that we are simply unable to prepare given this kind of work. Loshi Liri was supposed to testify tomorrow, and he will now testify two weeks later, and the witness who was supposed to testify in two weeks will be called tomorrow. And another thing, well, regardless of whether we might, in the end, be able to start with this witness, the witness Sweeney, well, it's impossible to prepare for him in such a short time, and we have five working days next week, and we have been preparing for the witnesses that were scheduled for next week. I think that I have presented our problem to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I, please, Your Honours. First, may I indicate that our request to alter the order arises from logistical difficulties in getting visas for some of the witnesses, or one witness in particular, a major witness, in particular, whose visa expired. And we have to expend some time in getting him another visa to attend. Apart from that I should add that the next witness, Liri Loshi, his attendance in this order, as it is, was conveyed to the Defence many days ago. I can't remember when; I'm trying to find that information. So the Defence has been aware for a long time that Liri Loshi -- that we're seeking to bring Liri Loshi forward. And in respect to this particular order of witnesses, I did speak with my friend about that yesterday, altering the order, and he expressed no objections. I showed him the order that we have there, because of the difficulties we're having, we would be bringing the witnesses forward. In order for the Court to have business to do next week, we would have to bring the witnesses who come or have visas and who could come, we would have to bring them forward and put off the remainder. And I did not confirm these arrangements until after I spoke to the Defence about it. But it is impossible to find the details as to -- yes, we have found that for Liri Loshi, this was indicated to the Defence on the 19th of January, that he would testify this week. So the Defence has been -- yes, we have an indication here, we have the filing here of the 19th of January, that Liri Loshi would be available for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But wasn't that an earlier notification which has been overtaken by more than one subsequent notification that didn't propose the witness Loshi for this coming week?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The subsequent notifications are -- were in respect to witnesses that were expected to come after Loshi, so they would not directly have affected what we stated about Loshi for this week. But I think the Defence's complaint is that the order has changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Defence's complaint boils down to the fact that they need time to prepare, and they have prepared for certain witnesses. It's now proposed not to call those witnesses but instead to call others who weren't listed to be heard at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, it is correct, and I'm explaining to you the reasons. Yes. It's a bit difficult to shuffle through all of the documents. And the real change is to bring forward Sweeney, Ramadani and Krasniqi earlier before K90, Malaj and Peraj, as had been earlier indicated. K90, Malaj, and Peraj are witnesses who deal with one particular crime scene. One of them would not be able to attend, although he was scheduled, because of visa difficulties; another of them had personal difficulties and will not be able to attend this week either. So we were left in a situation where we have no one for this week. As I indicated, Loshi had been indicated to the Defence from the 19th, in the order or the approximate order in which he was being -- in which we propose to take him. So the real issue for the Defence is bringing forward Sweeney, Ramadani, and Krasniqi. If are not in a position to bring him forward, we will not have the witnesses as we intended for the remainder of next week, after we take Loshi. Now, I understand the difficulties the Defence can have if there's a change -- change in the order. However, there are logistical difficulties that we have to -- we have to deal with as best as we can. And before I even forwarded what I did to the Defence, as I indicated, I showed it to them yesterday, and so I'm surprised now that the complaint is being made after we formally sent it to them today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, your proposition is that, if I can put them in order, your notification of the 13th of January, listed in the order in which they've been heard, four witnesses, but an additional witness was introduced, which is Mrs. Berisha. She came ahead of the last two witnesses. But even so, notification of her being called was given on the 19th of January. We then have on the 26th of January notification that you were to call during the week commencing the 9th of February Krasniqi, Ramadani, and Sweeney, three of the witnesses whom you have just indicated will be called during this coming week. But in addition, you have introduced in this latest notification the name of Loshi who was to have been called during the week commencing the 2nd of February but hasn't been reached. So that witness will now be called next week instead of this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, we -- if we finish with this witness tomorrow, we expect to call Loshi next, which is precisely what I am saying. There is no real change in order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The point I'm making is that he was to be called this week on your notification of the 19th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it was your notification of the 26th of January that first mentioned Krasniqi, Ramadani and Sweeney, who are, because they've not been reached, now to be heard, you hope, during this coming week commencing the 9th of February. That leaves us, then, with the witnesses K90, who had been in your notification of the 19th of January for this week but who has not been reached. It also includes the witness Malaj. And Malaj was in the notification of the 19th of January for this last week, or this week, and the witness Peraj, who was also in your notification of the 19th of January. Well, the witness names seem to have been the subject of notification on either the 19th of January or the 26th of January, but what has happened is a change in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. There is no legitimate complaint in respect to timely notification as to when they will testify. What has happened is that because of the time some of the witnesses have taken, witnesses who have particular problems have had to -- we have had to make changes in respect to them, the order. That is all, the order has been changed around a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You said a witness didn't have a visa or it had expired.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It expired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that witness on the list for next week or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think that witness was on the list for this week. And that witness, we expected, would have occupied a couple of days this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that K90?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'd prefer not to indicate his name with respect to his visa issues. But that is not the person. He had a visa for this week, but since he wasn't reached, the visa is about to expire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. I know the problem prevented by the governmental administration from the country from which they come. The visas are issued only for a week, and if somehow they are not reached, there is no visa, and it often takes, in my experience, two or three weeks to get another visa. I'm aware of that problem. It's a familiar one. You said earlier you felt there was no legitimate complaint. I think you must accept, Mr. Stamp, that there is legitimacy in a complaint that if counsel have prepared for certain witnesses, for whatever the reason, if that witness order is changed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... it can be extremely disruptive, if not practical, for Defence counsel to be prepared for cross-examination. As a typical example, and I don't know whether it has arisen here, and I don't look for an answer. It may be that it was arranged that one counsel would deal with witnesses X, Y, and Z, and you changed the order so that that counsel is not here on the days you're calling X, Y, and Z, that sort of thing. The Chamber is well aware that you can have logistical problems, but you need also to be aware that your logistical problems will create logistical problems for the Defence and in turn can create logistical problems for the Chamber. So that matters of that nature have to be given close attention, and the moment it is apparent that there will need to be some change, there needs to be an immediate notification in the hope that the Defence will be able to adjust their arrangements to accommodate your difficulty. Now, is there anything else you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I fully accept what Your Honour has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'll turn back now, if I may, to Mr. Djurdjic. None of the witnesses to be called next week on this latest notification appear to be new witnesses that have just been introduced, Mr. Djurdjic. They've each been the subject of notifications for either the 19th of January or the 26th of January, and what has really happened is the changing of order. Is that a correct understanding that I have so far?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to say something about one of the things that the Prosecutor said. It is true that we discussed the order yesterday, but the order was Gjogaj Ali, Mustafa Dragaj, Liri Loshi. I wanted to know whether the next one up was Nike Peraj and when he would be appearing for the sake of my preparation. But there was nothing said at all about John Sweeney or any other witnesses, nor was there any reference to a change in the witness order. What is of concern to me is, firstly, you know that we are facing a lot of difficulty concerning the translations of our documents. Seven days before we started our cross-examination, we are due to hand over our documents for inspection in order to have them ready for our cross. Therefore, it is true that all these witnesses and the order were brought to our attention weeks ahead, but now we had -- John Sweeney was supposed to be appearing in the week after the 9th, and we are facing the possibility that he might be appearing at witness number 1 next Monday, and then again K22 has just been announced. My colleague Marie O'Leary has just told me about the change related to K25 which was not announced. We cannot have a full five-day working week next week. The Defence simply can't cope with this kind of change in the witness order and all these changes from week to week. We can't prepare properly, nor, indeed, can we obtain the required translations. As for Liri, alright, we expected him this week, but John Sweeney was not scheduled at all. And the order was supposed to be exactly the other way around. So number 4, number 5, now becomes number 1, number 3, number 2, and number 1, number 4. This is creating a whole lot of problems for us because we work according to the notice we had served on us by the OTP, and we take that to be the schedule. I don't think we can go on like this. As for John Sweeney, the Defence cannot possibly prepare for our cross-examination to commence next Monday. We have five working days scheduled for next week. That's another thing that we need to bear in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I only have four. Oh, there's the possibility of the afternoon of Wednesday, the 11th. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just rise to suggest, if I may, that we could, with the leave of the Court, try to put on Sweeney, not on Monday but on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Stamp, but I think we're going to have to pull some of these problems together and try and avoid them. Part of the problem is not one of yours but one of the Defence, in that they are trying to get translations made so that they can use them in cross-examination, if I understand Mr. Djurdjic correctly. And for that reason priority is being given to the witnesses in the order that they've been shown on your list. And then when you change the order, Mr. Djurdjic and his lead counsel find themselves without the documents that they need for cross-examination because they, the translations, are being prepared in the earlier order, not the latest order that you propose. Now, it's not clear to me why you have a significant problem over the next intended witness, Loshi, Mr. Djurdjic. Is there a particular problem about preparation for that witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. We are ready for Witness Loshi. He was scheduled for next week. No problem with that. We have a problem with Sweeney and the order of all the other witnesses, the order that was reshuffled, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's our problem. As for Loshi, Liri, Mr. Stamp is right, that was supposed to be this way, and we agreed yesterday that he would be appearing after Mustafa Dragaj. But Sweeny came up all of a sudden, and then K25. I don't know if that was announced to you, if got a notice of that. Now all of a sudden K25 pops up, and I don't think that was ever scheduled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the Chamber's view, this is a larger than usual teething problem, as we are moving into a new trial, but that it's a problem which we think can be overcome by some modification. What we propose is that tomorrow, when the present witness has finished, the next witness called should be Loshi. But this afternoon and, if necessary, further tomorrow afternoon, we want counsel to confer and a list re-ordered that is one that can be managed both by Prosecution and Defence for the coming week. If a solution can't be found, the Chamber will have to determine the list, and that may be inconvenient to both counsel. But at the moment it seems, from what we have heard, that it should be possible for the problems of each counsel to be reasonably reconciled so that we can develop an order of witnesses for next week which both can manage. And that, once that is achieved, ought to carry on for the following week, because I think it will take us two weeks to work our way out of this present difficulty. Now, can the Chamber ask counsel to give attention to that this afternoon in a joint meeting, approached I hope with an awareness by each counsel of the problems of the other so that we can come to a list which will be manageable during the coming week, and then for the following week, which is, of course, only a three-day sitting week. If there are continuing problems tomorrow, the Chamber will hear them, and we may have to come up with a solution that may not be readily suited to either counsel. So it would be very much in everybody's interests if you can accommodate each other's difficulties. We now adjourn, and we resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 6th day of February, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.10 p.m.,
